properties.natural_language: Before validating excess_blob_gas in a block header, the block producer (SEMI_TRUSTED) must have produced a header where excess_blob_gas matches the result of calc_excess_blob_gas with the updated formula including fork activation timestamp logic.

The block header received for validation must include both the parent header and the current block timestamp, as these are required inputs for the excess_blob_gas calculation under the updated formula.
A semi-trusted block producer's header values are not accepted at face value; the validation action must independently recalculate excess_blob_gas and reject any mismatch.
Rollups must independently adjust their blob pricing algorithms to account for the higher minimum fee (2^25 wei); no protocol-level coordination mechanism exists for this adjustment.

The approximately 5.9 blocks doubling rate is derived from the existing EIP-4844 exponential formula with the new minimum base fee parameter; the specification does not independently verify this derivation.
All clients must implement the fork activation reset (excess_blob_gas to zero) correctly and synchronously; failure causes chain splits through invalid block production or valid block rejection.
Rollups are assumed to have sufficient reserves or quick-adjustment capability to handle the increased minimum blob fees without service disruption.
The minimum fee level of 2^25 wei is assumed appropriate for market conditions and will not cause excessive costs during low demand periods.

After calculating excess blob gas, the result must account for fork activation: if the parent block is pre-fork and the current block meets or exceeds the fork timestamp, excess_blob_gas is reset to zero.
After computing the blob base fee, the result must be at least MIN_BASE_FEE_PER_BLOB_GAS (2^25 wei = 33,554,432 wei), enforced by the minimum floor constraint.
After validation, the block header is in exactly one of two states: valid (excess_blob_gas matches) or invalid (excess_blob_gas mismatch, block rejected).
After detecting a fork boundary, the one-time reset sets excess_blob_gas to zero and transitions to the post-fork state with new pricing parameters.
The blob base fee can never be less than MIN_BASE_FEE_PER_BLOB_GAS (2^25 wei) for any block after fork activation.
Before the BLAKE2 F precompile processes any input, the caller (UNTRUSTED) must have submitted data via a CALL to address 0x09. All input data is untrusted and must be validated.
The precompile must validate that input is exactly 213 bytes before any parsing occurs. Inputs of any other length must cause the precompile to fail.
The final block flag (f) byte from untrusted input must be exactly 0x00 or 0x01; any other value causes the precompile to fail with all gas consumed.
Invalid f flag values cause the precompile to return empty output with all gas consumed, consistent with other precompile error behavior, though the exact error type is not specified.
Input byte boundaries follow consecutive layout: rounds[0:4], h[4:68], m[68:196], t0[196:204], t1[204:212], f[212:213], totaling exactly 213 bytes.
The implementation of BLAKE2 F function must match RFC 7693 exactly; any deviation could break interoperability with off-chain BLAKE2 implementations.
No crafted input can cause the BLAKE2 F computation to produce incorrect cryptographic outputs; the function is deterministic given valid inputs.
GFROUND = 1 gas per round must provide sufficient cost to prevent DoS attacks via excessive rounds values (up to 2^32 - 1).
After input length validation, the precompile is in exactly one of two states: length valid (proceed to parsing) or length invalid (precompile fails).
After BLAKE2 F compression execution, the output is the updated h state vector encoded as exactly 64 bytes in little-endian format.
After gas cost computation, the required gas equals rounds * GFROUND (where GFROUND = 1). If available gas is insufficient, the call fails.
After complete input validation, the f flag is verified as boolean (0 or 1). Validation passes only if both length and flag checks succeed.
The BLAKE2 F precompile input must always be exactly 213 bytes; this invariant is enforced at the entry point before any field extraction occurs.
Before a proposal enters the routing system, the proposal author (SEMI_TRUSTED) must have submitted a draft. The scope classification is performed by editors, not the author.
Proposal classification must determine whether the change affects core protocol (routed to EIP repo) or application layer (routed to ERC repo) before number assignment.
Legacy URL requests from untrusted users must be checked to determine if the resource has been migrated to the ERC repository, with appropriate redirects issued for migrated content.
The boundary between core protocol and application layer changes is determined by whether the change would be discussed in AllCoreDevs calls; edge cases require editorial judgment.
Proposals spanning both core protocol and application layers should be split into separate EIP and ERC documents, or classified based on primary impact.
EIP editors can consistently and accurately classify proposals; misclassification leads to proposals in the wrong repository, causing implementer confusion.
Existing tools and documentation referencing ERC URLs will eventually be updated to use ercs.ethereum.org; perpetual redirect reliance risks breakage if infrastructure is deprecated.
After classification, a proposal is routed to exactly one repository: either EIP (even number, core protocol) or ERC (odd number, application layer).
After URL type checking, a legacy URL request results in either an HTTP redirect to ercs.ethereum.org (if migrated ERC) or serving the EIP content directly.
Before an EIP enters the eligibility lifecycle, the EIP author (SEMI_TRUSTED) must have created and submitted a draft. The author's proposal requires ACD consensus before advancement.
An EIP author must request a discussion slot at AllCoreDevs before the EIP can be evaluated; no EIP can bypass the ACD discussion requirement.
Rough consensus means a clear majority of active core developers agree, without formal voting requirements, following IETF-style consensus determination.
Eligibility revocation follows the same ACD consensus process that granted it, though this process is not explicitly documented in the specification.
Well-written implementation PRs must follow client codebase conventions, include tests, and properly implement the specification to qualify for acceptance.
Core developers participating in ACD calls must represent the interests of the Ethereum ecosystem broadly; governance capture would enable harmful EIP approval.
ACD meeting notes must accurately capture consensus decisions and reasoning; inaccurate notes could lead to disputes about EIP status.
The EIP governance process depends on continued volunteer participation from client developers; loss of key participants would break the governance process.
After core devs vote, the EIP is in exactly one of two states: eligible for inclusion (rough consensus achieved) or returned to draft (consensus not achieved).
After eligibility validation, all three criteria must be met: conceptual support, implementation willingness, and documentation link; failure of any criterion results in validation failure.
After successful testing, the EIP is assigned to a specific hard fork with an activation block; after fork activation, the EIP is deployed on mainnet.
After consensus assessment, the decision (approval or deferral) must be documented in meeting notes with a link to the EIP.
Before the wallet processes a Type 1 transaction, the user or dapp (UNTRUSTED) submits a transaction for signing. The wallet must automatically detect and convert Type 1 to Type 2.
The untrusted user's Type 1 transaction data must be fully preserved during conversion: access_list is copied unchanged, gas_price is mapped to both max_fee_per_gas and max_priority_fee_per_gas.
Both max_fee_per_gas and max_priority_fee_per_gas are set equal to the original gas_price value, as the exact mapping is not specified in the EIP.
The conversion from Type 1 to Type 2 is automatic and transparent; wallets MUST convert and should not offer an option to preserve Type 1 format.
The chain_id field is preserved unchanged during the Type 1 to Type 2 conversion, maintaining replay protection.
The network must support EIP-1559 and Type 2 transactions (London fork or later); converted transactions would be rejected by pre-London nodes.
Users submitting Type 1 transactions are assumed to accept automatic conversion to Type 2 without explicit consent.
The wallet must perform the conversion correctly without modifying transaction intent; incorrect conversion results in different gas economics than intended.
No security benefit is lost by deprecating Type 1 in favor of Type 2; there are no edge cases where Type 1 offered security properties absent in Type 2.
After conversion, the Type 2 transaction has type field 0x2, the original access_list, and max_fee_per_gas/max_priority_fee_per_gas derived from the original gas_price.
After field mapping, the Type 2 transaction retains all original transaction fields except gas_price (replaced by two EIP-1559 fee fields) and type (changed to 0x2).
After fee conversion, the user's transaction is eligible for EIP-1559 benefits including potential refund if the base fee is lower than max_fee_per_gas.
After signing the converted Type 2 transaction, the signature covers the new transaction format including EIP-1559 fee fields.
Before the RLPx handshake begins, the initiating peer (UNTRUSTED) provides static and ephemeral keys. The receiving node must verify identity through ECIES decryption with its static private key.
Auth packets from untrusted peers must be ECIES-encrypted with the recipient's static public key; only the intended recipient can decrypt them.
Hello packets from untrusted remote peers are parsed with forward-compatible tolerance: version mismatches are ignored, and additional list elements are accepted.
UDP discovery packets from untrusted peers must not exceed 1280 bytes; oversized packets are rejected before parsing.
Discovery packets with unknown packet types from untrusted peers must be silently discarded without error propagation.
Auth packet padding of 100-300 random bytes must use cryptographically secure random data to prevent traffic analysis attacks.
Silent discard of unknown packet types means no error response is sent to the sender; local logging may occur for debugging purposes.
When simultaneous connection attempts use different protocol formats (v4 vs EIP-8), the receiving node determines format from packet structure and responds in the same format.
ECIES encryption with the recipient's static public key ensures only the intended recipient can decrypt auth/ack packets; MITM attacks are prevented.
Attackers cannot generate valid signatures without the initiator's private key; connection hijacking or impersonation is not possible.
All future protocol versions must maintain backward compatibility with the RLP structure requirements established by EIP-8.
The 1280 byte discovery packet size limit is sufficient for all current and future discovery message types.
After auth packet generation, the packet contains signature, initiator-pubk, initiator-nonce, auth-vsn=4, and 100-300 bytes of random padding, encrypted with ECIES.
After tolerant auth body parsing, required fields (signature, nonces, public keys) are extracted while version mismatches, additional list elements, and trailing data are ignored.
After both auth and ack packets are exchanged, both parties can derive session keys for encrypted communication.
After tolerant hello parsing, the connection is established regardless of version differences; the node responds with its highest supported devp2p version.
After discovery packet parsing, recognized packet types are processed normally while unrecognized types are silently discarded.
After validation, packets pass only if required fields (signature, nonces, public keys) are present; version checks are skipped and extra elements ignored per EIP-8 rules.
The RLPx protocol must never reject a peer solely due to protocol version mismatch; forward compatibility is maintained through tolerant parsing.
After popping both operands, the comparison is executed based on the selected opcode: LT (unsigned <), SLT (signed <), GT (unsigned >), SGT (signed >), or EQ (==).
After any comparison execution, the boolean result is converted to U256: true becomes U256(1), false becomes U256(0), which is pushed onto the stack.
After the comparison result is pushed, the program counter is incremented by 1 and the instruction is complete, ready for the next opcode.
After ISZERO execution, if the popped value equals zero the result is U256(1), otherwise U256(0); this is pushed to the stack.
After attempting to charge GAS_VERY_LOW, execution either proceeds (sufficient gas) or halts with an out-of-gas exception.
If fewer than the required number of operands exist on the stack, a StackUnderflowError is raised following standard EVM convention.
The first popped value is the left operand and the second is the right operand; comparison is left op right where left is stack[0] and right is stack[1].
The EVM must have at least the required number of operands on the stack before executing comparison instructions; stack underflow halts execution.
The .to_signed() conversion must correctly handle 256-bit two's complement representation for SLT and SGT operations.
GAS_VERY_LOW constant is set to an appropriate value that prevents denial of service through comparison operation spam.
All comparison opcodes (LT, GT, SLT, SGT, EQ, ISZERO) produce exactly one stack output value that is either U256(0) or U256(1); no other output values are possible.
Binary comparison instructions consume exactly 2 stack elements and produce 1; ISZERO consumes exactly 1 and produces 1. Net stack effect is -1 or 0 respectively.
Raw transaction bytes from an untrusted submitter must be decoded by inspecting the first byte to determine transaction type before any processing occurs.
Transaction signature validation requires 0 < r < SECP256K1N and 0 < s <= SECP256K1N/2 (low-s requirement) before public key recovery is attempted.
After transaction type detection, the transaction is classified as exactly one of: Legacy (first byte >= 0xc0), Type 1 (0x01), Type 2 (0x02), Type 3 (0x03), or Type 4 (0x04).
After validation, a transaction passes only if gas >= max(intrinsic_cost, floor_cost), nonce < 2^64-1, and init code (if any) <= MAX_INIT_CODE_SIZE.
After signature recovery, the sender address is derived by taking keccak256 of the recovered public key and extracting the rightmost 20 bytes.
After intrinsic gas calculation, the total includes base cost (21000) + calldata cost + create cost (if applicable) + access list cost + authorization cost (if SetCode).
After signing hash computation, the hash is type-specific: pre-EIP155 (v in {27,28}), EIP-155 (with chain_id), or typed transaction (with type prefix byte).
After EIP-7623 floor gas calculation, the effective gas requirement is max(intrinsic_cost, floor_cost) where floor_cost = (total_tokens * FLOOR_CALLDATA_COST) + TX_BASE_COST.
In calldata context, a 'token' refers to a single byte: zero bytes cost 0 gas, non-zero bytes cost STANDARD_CALLDATA_TOKEN_COST (4 gas).
Authorization cost for SetCodeTransaction follows EIP-7702 which defines separate costs for new vs existing accounts in the authorization list.
The low-s requirement (s <= SECP256K1N/2) prevents signature malleability attacks per BIP-62, ensuring transaction uniqueness.
RLP decoding must correctly reject malformed transaction data; parsing failures prevent further processing.
The SECP256K1N constant and secp256k1 curve parameters must be correctly implemented across all clients.
Low-s enforcement prevents signature malleability attacks, ensuring transaction uniqueness and replay protection.
MAX_INIT_CODE_SIZE must balance allowing legitimate contract deployments while preventing DoS through extremely large init code.
Every valid transaction must have a recoverable sender address; transactions with invalid signatures are always rejected.
Prague supports exactly five transaction types: Legacy (0), Access List (1), Fee Market (2), Blob (3), and SetCode (4). Any other type byte is invalid.
RPC responses from untrusted providers must include cryptographic proofs that can be verified against known state roots before data is accepted.
The response payload and Merkle proof from an untrusted RPC provider must both be present for verification; missing proofs result in rejection.
Data from an untrusted provider is never accepted until the proof has been successfully verified; invalid proofs trigger rejection and malicious provider detection.
Each component EIP referenced by this meta-EIP is independently specified; this EIP defines overall coordination strategy only.
Completeness proofs must demonstrate that no additional matching data exists beyond what was returned in the response.
EIP-7792 (ZK-verified log index root) and EIP-7745 (2D log index) are alternative approaches; implementations choose one or the other.
Light clients must have access to verified state roots (e.g., from consensus layer) to validate proofs; without trusted roots, the entire proof system is insecure.
SSZ libraries must be available and production-grade across all execution clients; uneven quality could cause consensus issues.
Backward compatibility with RLP/JSON-RPC patterns must be maintained during the transition to SSZ/binary API.
Attackers cannot forge SSZ Merkle proofs without knowing the underlying data; the cryptographic security of the proof system must hold.
After proof verification, the data is in exactly one of two states: trusted (proof valid, data accepted) or rejected (proof invalid, provider flagged as malicious).
After SSZ conversion and root computation, partial proofs can be generated for specific fields without requiring the full data object.
After receipt normalization, all fields needed for independent verification (including logIndex and individual gasUsed) are present in the SSZ representation.
After native ETH transfer, a system-emitted log event makes the transfer visible in log data, enabling tracking equivalent to ERC-20 transfers.
After implementing the binary API, blob data can be transmitted in native binary format without ASCII hex-encoding overhead, and data can be served directly from database without decompression.
After building the 2D log index, clients can query logs with bounded false-positive rates and receive results with completeness proofs, replacing the legacy bloom filter.
The client never trusts RPC provider data without proof verification; all accepted data has been cryptographically verified against known state roots.
Before linting runs, the EIP contributor (SEMI_TRUSTED) must have submitted a pull request through GitHub. The contributor's changes are subject to automated and manual review.
The linter must determine if the PR changes the EIP status field to decide whether to enforce lint rules on all lines (status change) or only touched lines (no status change).
SHOULD NOT implies strong recommendation but allows exceptions at maintainer discretion; this is not a strict requirement.
All existing linting rules apply uniformly regardless of status change; the distinction is only about scope (all lines vs touched lines only).
EIP editors and tooling maintainers are assumed to implement the relaxed linting scope as specified, reducing barriers to micro-contributions.
This meta-governance EIP has no impact on Ethereum protocol runtime behavior; it only affects the EIP editorial process.
After status change detection, full-document lint enforcement is applied; all lint errors in the document must be fixed before the PR can merge.
After confirming no status change, only touched-line lint enforcement is applied; lint errors in untouched lines do not block the PR.
